text: 1 · Linear models and naive Bayes Linear regression predicts a numeric target as ŷ = w T x + b and is fitted by least squares, minimising the mean squared error; the closed form is w = ( X T X ) −1 X T y , the maximum-likelihood fit under Gaussian noise (the losses and their noise models are on Loss functions ).
label: core

text: Polynomial regression is the same model on powers and products of the features: still linear in the weights.
label: core

text: The regularised variants add a penalty: ridge (L2, λΣ w 2 , shrinks every weight), lasso (L1, λΣ| w |, sets some weights exactly to zero) and elastic net (both); how and why they work, with the geometry, is on Regularisation .
label: owned:models_and_training/topic_ml_fundamentals/regularisation

text: Logistic regression is a linear model, a sigmoid and binary cross entropy: p ( y = 1 | x ) = σ( w T x + b ), so the weights act additively on the log-odds and the decision boundary is a straight line (a hyperplane).
label: core
key: the weights act additively on the log-odds

text: Softmax regression (multinomial logistic regression) is the multiclass version: one weight vector per class and a softmax. scikit-learn's LogisticRegression is L2-penalised by default with C = 1, minimising ½|| w || 2 + CΣ log-loss ( user guide ), a default worth knowing when a "plain" logistic regression shrinks its weights.
label: core

text: Try it on circles in the lab: no straight line separates a ring from its centre unless the features are transformed first.
label: core
key: cannot enclose a ring unless the features are transformed first

text: Naive Bayes applies Bayes' rule with the assumption that features are independent given the class: p ( y | x ) ∝ p ( y ) ∏ j p ( x j | y ).
label: core
key: assuming the features independent given the class

text: Each factor is estimated separately (word frequencies per class for text, a Gaussian per feature for numbers), so training is one counting pass.
label: core

text: The assumption is almost never true, yet the classifier is a strong, cheap baseline for text: on short snippets it beat SVMs in Wang and Manning's comparison, and their NBSVM (an SVM on naive Bayes log-count ratios) was a strong text baseline for years ( Wang and Manning 2012 ).
label: core

text: The generative model reaches its best error with fewer examples, though a discriminative model such as logistic regression ends lower with enough data ( Ng and Jordan 2002 ).
label: core

text: Its probabilities are overconfident when features are correlated, because the same evidence is counted several times; recalibrate before using them (the calibration animation on Evaluation metrics does exactly this to a real naive Bayes model).
label: core

text: 2 · Decision trees A decision tree asks one yes/no question about one feature at a time ("is mean radius ≤ 0.43?") and predicts, in each leaf, the majority class or the mean target of the training points that reach it.
label: core

text: It is grown greedily, CART style ( Breiman, Friedman, Olshen and Stone 1984 ): at each node, try every feature and every threshold between two neighbouring distinct values (scikit-learn uses the midpoint), and keep the split that lowers the weighted impurity of the two children most.
label: core

text: Gini = 1 − Σ k p k 2 entropy = −Σ k p k log 2 p k gain = I (parent) − ( n L / n ) I (left) − ( n R / n ) I (right) p k share of class k among the node's training points; for regression, I is the variance of the targets (squared error) Greedy means one step ahead only: a split that is useless by itself but makes the next one perfect ( XOR, in the lab ) can be missed at depth 1.
label: core

text: Unlimited, the tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure, so it can fit any training set exactly; its predictions then change a lot when a few training points change (high variance).
label: core

text: 5 · Support vector machines A support vector machine ( Cortes and Vapnik 1995 ) looks for the separating hyperplane with the widest margin : the band, of width 2/|| w || between the lines where the score w T x + b equals ±1, that it keeps clear of training points.
label: core

text: Real data are rarely separable, so the soft margin lets points into the band at a price set by C: min ½|| w || 2 + C Σ i max(0, 1 − y i ( w T x i + b )) y i ∈ {−1, +1} max(0, 1 − m) the hinge loss on the margin m = y · f ( x ): zero once a point is beyond its side's margin line; compared with logistic and exponential losses on Loss functions ("One axis for every classification loss: the margin") C the inverse of the L2 penalty's strength: small C, wide margin and many violations; large C, every violation expensive The solution depends only on dot products between points, and only on the points on or inside the margin, the support vectors : in the dual problem every other point has weight α i = 0, and the score is f ( x ) = Σ α i y i K ( x i , x ) + b with 0 ≤ α i ≤ C.
label: core

text: The kernel trick replaces the dot product with a kernel K , a dot product in a feature space that is never built: the RBF kernel exp(−γ|| x − x ′|| 2 ) corresponds to an infinite-dimensional one, and the polynomial kernel ( x T x ′ + c ) d to all monomials up to degree d . γ sets how far one point's influence reaches; scikit-learn's default, "scale", is 1/(number of features × variance of X ).
label: core

text: The page's SVM is the same solver family as libsvm: sequential minimal optimisation, which changes two αs at a time, with libsvm's second-order rule for choosing the pair ( Fan, Chen and Lin 2005 ).

text: 6 · Nearest neighbours k nearest neighbours has no training step: it stores the training set and, for a query, returns the majority class (or the mean target) of the k closest points. k and the distance are its hyperparameters: k = 1 reproduces every training label (zero training error, a jagged boundary), a large k smooths towards the overall majority; try both in the lab .

text: 7 · Clustering Method One-liner Watch out k-means alternate: assign each point to its nearest centre, move each centre to the mean of its points; minimises the within-cluster sum of squares (inertia) you choose k (elbow or silhouette); assumes round clusters of similar size; depends on the start (use k-means++ and several restarts) Hierarchical (agglomerative) start with every point alone and repeatedly merge the two closest clusters by a linkage: single (closest pair), complete (farthest pair), average, or Ward (smallest increase in variance); cut the dendrogram at the level you want the pairwise distances alone take O( n 2 ) memory and the classic algorithm O( n 3 ) time (O( n 2 ) for single linkage, Sibson 1973 ); the linkage changes the answer DBSCAN density: points with at least minPts neighbours within eps are core points; clusters are what core points reach; the rest is noise ( Ester et al.
label: depth
key: minimises the within-cluster sum of squares

text: 1996 ) finds any shape and needs no k , but one eps must suit every cluster's density Gaussian mixture + EM soft clustering: each cluster a Gaussian with its own weight, mean and covariance; EM alternates responsibilities (E) and parameter updates (M) ( Dempster, Laird and Rubin 1977 ) local optima; k still chosen (BIC helps); covariances can collapse onto a single point without regularisation Lloyd's iteration can only lower the inertia, so it always stops, but at a local minimum that depends on the start. k-means++ picks each new starting centre with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest centre already chosen; its expected inertia is within a factor O(log k ) of the optimum before any iteration ( Arthur and Vassilvitskii 2007 ). scikit-learn uses a greedy variant that tries 2 + ⌊ln k ⌋ candidates per centre and keeps the best ( KMeans ); the page uses the plain rule.

text: 8 · Anomaly detection Anomalies are rare, so this is usually unsupervised: model what normal looks like and flag what does not fit.
label: core

text: Isolation forest ( Liu, Ting and Zhou 2008 ) builds random trees that split on a random feature at a random value; an anomaly, being few and different, is isolated in few splits.
label: core

text: The score is s = 2 −E[ h ( x )]/ c ( n ) , where h is the path length to isolate x and c ( n ) = 2 H ( n − 1) − 2( n − 1)/ n the average path length of an unsuccessful search in a binary search tree ( H the harmonic number): s near 1 is anomalous, well below 0.5 normal.
label: core
key: unsuccessful search in a binary search tree

text: It needs no distances, so it scales to large, high-dimensional data.
